newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Electrolux H1 loss seen as start of revamp.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Electrolux H1 loss seen as start of revamp.

text.p: Electrolux, the world's largest supplier of household appliances, on Wednesday posted a loss for the first half of 1997 due to a hefty restructuring programme designed to spin the company around.

The company reported a loss of 264 million crowns ($32.7 million) after taking into account a capital gain of 604 million from the sale of Husqvarna Sewing Machines and a 2.5 billion crown revamp aimed at halting more than two sluggish years for Electrolux.
Analysts, aware restructuring costs would be charged against second quarter earnings, said the report was mixed but the key thing was to see that changes were now underway.
The tough two-year plan, unveiled by new chief executive Michael Treschow in June, involves closing 25 plants, 50 warehouses and axing 12,000 jobs, 11 percent of the workforce.
"We do not expect to see any real benefit this year but next year we hope to see some results," Schroeder analyst Susan Anthony told Reuters.

"They are making good progress despite the holiday period in identifying where jobs are at risk and we hope to keep seeing news on various measures being agreed to feel the momentum is building up and things are really happening."
The Swedish whitegoods giant indicated sparks of improvement in income and in some key markets, particularly in the second quarter of 1997.

"It was encouraging to see that commercial appliances were back in profit, good to see progress in the U.S. on the white goods side and repositioning their brand going ahead as hoped and outdoor products steaming ahead," said one analyst.
However operating profits from its key white goods division were still below last year's levels despite some improvements in the U.S. and parts of Europe which was a disappointment.

Electrolux said pre-tax income, excluding non-recurring items, was on a level with the previous year while group sales inched up 0.5 percent to 57.27 billion crowns in the first half, rising five percent in the second quarter.

"Demand for white goods in Europe rose during the second quarter...mainly due to Italy, Spain and Scandinavia while conditions remained weak in Germany, Britain and France," Treschow said in a statement.
A decrease in operating income in Brazil in the second quarter due to a slump in demand was also disappointing but a recovery was expected over the rest of the year, Treschow said.

He was more optimistic about the U.S. market, where rivals Whirlpool and General Electric dominate the market, saying demand had been at high levels in most the group's product areas so far this year.
"I think we will earn money from our operations in the U.S. this year and we haven't done this for a long time," he said.

Despite the slight improvements, the half year operating income for the white goods division of 1.15 billion crowns was lower than 1.20 billion in the first half of 1996 and also lower in the second quarter this year than a year ago.
Treschow said the third quarter had started well but he voiced concern about Germany which accounts for about 30 percent of Electrolux's white good sales in Europe.
"The most worrying thing on the horizon is Germany and there we are seeing no sign of any improvement," Treschow told a news conference.
"It is not only what happens with demand but we are also seeing a trend towards cheaper and cheaper products."
Treschow stressed the importance of the restructuring programme that is designed to halt the company's ailing profits and falling market share.
The revamp was welcomed by the market and Electrolux's share price soared on the announcement from 465 crown to a record high of 670 crowns. It closed four lower at 611 on Wednesday.
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1017 ($ = 8.063 Swedish Crowns)
